Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Basic Front-End Interaction
Basic Front-End Interaction
Connect wallets, get Provider and Signer, call contracts safely from the browser.
In this lesson

You will wire window.ethereum to an ethers.js Web3Provider, obtain a signer, attach an ABI and address, and make read and write calls with clear UX for confirmations and errors.

Why it matters

Front-end integration is the bridge between your contract logic and real users. Correct handling of providers, signers and transaction lifecycle prevents bad UX and security mistakes.

Explore Key Topics
Wallet Connect
Detect window.ethereum and request accounts.
Provider & Signer
Provider for reads, Signer for signed transactions.
Read vs Write
View calls are free; state changes create transactions and must be awaited.
Visual: Browser -> Wallet -> Contract
Browser
Contains your dApp. Loads ethers.js and code that requests the user to connect their wallet.
Wallet (MetaMask)
Exposes window.ethereum and performs secure signing inside the extension or mobile app.
Contract (ABI + Address)
The ABI tells ethers.js which functions exist and how to encode calls to the deployed address.

screens.title: What Web3.js and Ethers.js do
screens.narratorSegment: Client-side libraries provide the glue your dApp needs to talk to the blockchain without exposing private keys. Ethers. js and Web3. js provide utilities to encode function calls, decode results, format values, and to route requests through a provider that speaks to the network. In the browser context they rely on a provider implementation surfaced by the user's wallet, commonly available as window. ethereum. A provider is effectively a read-only gateway that can query chain data and fetch on-chain state without requesting a signature. A signer is a thin wrapper around an account that can propose transactions and sign them inside the wallet. This separation matters: reads are cheap and immediate, writes require user confirmation and produce transactions that must be mined. A common misconception is that ethers. js holds keys for you on the client; it does not. In the browser, signing always occurs inside the wallet extension or mobile app. To ground this, imagine an online bank: the provider is like a public ledger viewer, the signer is like the customer approving a wire transfer in their secure banking app. The core insight is to treat the wallet as the secure signer and the library as a safe translator between your UI and that signer.

keyIdea.title: Libraries vs wallets
keyIdea.text: Libraries encode and submit calls; the wallet provides the account and performs signing securely.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › What Web3.js and Ethers.js do
Client libraries explained
What they provide and how they rely on a wallet provider.
Definition

A library encodes ABI calls, formats values, and routes requests to a provider. It does not store the user's private keys in the browser wallet flow.

Key distinction
  • Provider: query chain state and perform read-only calls.
  • Signer: requests wallet to sign transactions for state changes.
Key Takeaway

Use libraries to translate and wallets to sign. Never store or expose private keys in front-end code.

Analogy: Bank Viewer vs Secure Approval

A provider is like a public ledger viewer that shows balances and transactions. A signer is like the secure mobile banking app that the user opens to approve a transfer.

Provider
Can read state and call view functions without a signature.
Signer
Can sign transactions; prompts the user to confirm in their wallet.
Common misconception
Developers sometimes assume the library stores keys. In browser flows signing always happens inside the wallet and the library only prepares the transaction payload.

screens.title: Detecting and Connecting a Wallet
screens.narratorSegment: The first live step in most dApps is establishing a connection to the user's wallet. Start by checking whether window. ethereum exists. If it does not, the user likely has no Web3 wallet installed and you should surface a clear message. If it exists, call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user to connect. The promise resolves with an array of addresses when the user approves, or throws when the user rejects. This pattern keeps your app defensive and prevents runtime errors like 'cannot read request of undefined.' After successful connection, enable UI controls and instantiate a provider and signer. Remember to handle both success and failure: on rejection show a helpful message and offer a retry, and when accepted update the UI to show the connected address. Also register listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged so your app adapts when the user switches accounts or networks. This makes the dApp robust across real user actions and avoids stale signer references. A misconception to avoid is assuming connection is permanent — the user can disconnect or switch accounts at any time.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Detecting and Connecting a Wallet
Steps to connect
1
Check if window.ethereum exists to detect a wallet.
2
Call window.ethereum.request with method eth_requestAccounts.
3
On success, enable actions and create provider/signer; on failure, show a message.
4
Register accountsChanged and chainChanged listeners to handle runtime changes.
Example Guard
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
  await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
  // proceed to create provider/signer
} else {
  // show install wallet message
}
UX tips
  • Disable transaction controls until the user connects.
  • Show clear status messages: not connected, connecting, connected.
  • On rejection, provide retry and brief explanation of why the request is needed.
Check your understanding
Why is it important to check window.ethereum before requesting accounts? What happens if you don't?

screens.title: Provider and Signer in ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Once a user approves connection, instantiate a provider that routes RPC calls through the wallet, and obtain a signer to authorize transactions. In ethers. js the pattern is creating a Web3Provider from window. ethereum and then calling getSigner on it. The provider lets you call view functions and read chain data; the signer represents the currently selected account and can sign and send transactions. It is common to use the signer when creating a contract instance intended for writes, and to use the provider for read-only interactions. A frequent subtlety is that after accounts change, you should re-acquire the signer from the provider to reflect the new selected account. Another common misunderstanding is confusing the provider returned by a JSON-RPC node and the Web3Provider wrapped around window. ethereum. The latter goes through the user's wallet and therefore triggers the wallet UI for signing. In practice you will see code like const provider = new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum); const signer = provider. getSigner(); — this small pattern is foundational for secure front-end interactions. Provider and Signer in ethers.js means web3provider wraps window.ethereum for reads; getsigner provides the user's account for signing transactions inside the wallet.. In practical terms, instantiate web3provider and getsigner from window.ethereum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Provider and Signer in ethers.js
Code walkthrough
// After user connects
const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum);
const signer = provider.getSigner();

// For read-only calls
const readOnlyContract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, provider);

// For state-changing calls
const writableContract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signer);
Remember to re-create the signer if accountsChanged fires. The provider is safe to reuse for reads across the session.
Example
Use provider for getCount, and signer for increment so MetaMask prompts for confirmation.
Pro tip
If you only need reads, passing provider reduces unnecessary user prompts. Only attach signer when a write is required.

screens.title: Calling a view function (getCount)
screens.narratorSegment: Reading state from a contract is straightforward and free because view functions do not create transactions. With an ethers. Contract instance attached to a provider you can call the view function and update the UI with the returned value. For example, to show a simple Counter contract's current count, call the count function and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Handle errors such as network problems by wrapping calls in try/catch. Reads are typically fast and should be used to refresh UI state after transactions confirm, or periodically if your dApp requires near-real-time updates. A common pitfall is mistakenly creating the contract with a signer when you only need to read — this is not wrong, but it may trigger unwanted prompts if signer initialization requires user interaction. Keep read logic isolated and graceful: show a loading state while the read is in progress, show an error state if it fails, and never assume the read will always return immediately. This pattern gives users clear feedback and prevents confusing blank displays. Calling a view function (getCount) means attach the contract to a provider for free view calls; handle errors and show loading states for good ux.. In practical terms, read contract state without creating transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Calling a view function (getCount)
Code snippet
async function getCount() {
  try {
    const currentCount = await counterContract.count();
    document.getElementById('countDisplay').innerText = currentCount.toString();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error getting count:', error);
    document.getElementById('countDisplay').innerText = 'Error';
  }
}
Use provider-based contract instances for reads to avoid any signing prompts and to keep the UI responsive.
UX elements
  • Show a Loading state while awaiting the read call.
  • Handle and display errors clearly, not just in the console.
  • Refresh reads after tx.wait resolves to surface new state.
Example card
A dashboard button triggers getCount and updates the count display with the returned BigNumber string.

screens.title: Calling a state-changing function (increment)
screens.narratorSegment: Write operations change blockchain state and therefore create transactions that must be signed and mined. When you call an increment function that is nonpayable, ethers. js returns a TransactionResponse immediately after the user confirms in their wallet. This response does not mean the transaction is confirmed; it only means it was submitted. For a reliable UI, await tx. wait() so your code pauses until the transaction has been mined and included in a block. While waiting, show a pending status or spinner to inform the user. Handle errors and transaction rejections with try/catch and update the status accordingly. After the transaction confirms, call your read method to show the new on-chain state. A frequent problem is neglecting to await tx. wait, which leads to UI reads that show the old state because the transaction has not been mined yet. In the browser, always assume network latency and block times. By awaiting confirmation and giving clear status updates you keep user expectations aligned with on-chain reality. Calling a state-changing function (increment) means always wait for transaction confirmation with tx.wait to ensure ui reads match the blockchain state.. In practical terms, trigger transactions, await confirmation, and update ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Calling a state-changing function (increment)
Write call pattern
async function incrementCounter() {
  try {
    const tx = await counterContract.increment();
    await tx.wait();
    await getCount();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error incrementing counter:', error);
  }
}
Show a 'pending' message after tx is submitted and replace it with 'confirmed' after tx.wait resolves to avoid confusing the user.
Example scenario
User clicks Increment, MetaMask prompts for gas and confirmation, the app shows 'Incrementing... Confirm in MetaMask.', then waits for tx.wait and updates the count when confirmed.
Common mistake
Not awaiting tx.wait leads to stale reads and poor UX because your UI may refresh before the block containing the transaction is mined.

screens.title: Attaching ABI and Contract Address
screens.narratorSegment: To call functions on a deployed contract from the browser you need two pieces of information: the contract's address and its ABI. The ABI is the JSON description of the contract's functions and events — it tells ethers. js how to encode and decode calls. You can copy the ABI from your Hardhat artifacts folder and embed it in the front-end code or fetch it at runtime. With ethers. js create a contract instance using new ethers. Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signerOrProvider). If you pass a provider, the instance can perform read-only calls; if you pass a signer, the instance can send transactions that prompt the user to sign. A practical approach is to keep two instances or to pass the appropriate signer for the operation. Make sure the address points to the deployed contract on the same network the wallet is connected to; otherwise the calls will fail or return empty results. A frequent oversight is mismatching test network addresses: always verify network alignment between the wallet and the deployed contract. Attaching ABI and Contract Address means the abi defines the contract interface; the address targets the specific deployed instance. both are required for client-side interactions.. In practical terms, create a contract instance from abi and address to call functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Attaching ABI and Contract Address
Contract instantiation
const counterContract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signer);
// or for reads
const counterRead = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, provider);
Keep contractABI extracted from your build artifacts to ensure function signatures match the deployed bytecode.
Network alignment
Ensure the wallet is on the same network as the deployed contract (for example, Sepolia in this exercise). If networks mismatch, calls will fail or return unexpected values.
Scenario
A contract deployed to Sepolia will not be reachable if the user's wallet is on Mainnet. Prompt users to switch networks when necessary.

screens.title: Event Listeners: accountsChanged & chainChanged
screens.narratorSegment: Browser wallets can change their selected account or the active network at any time. To stay in sync, register listeners for both accountsChanged and chainChanged on window. ethereum. When accountsChanged emits, check whether the accounts array is empty — this means the user disconnected — or update your signer and re-attach any contract instances tied to the account. When chainChanged occurs, you may need to reload the app or re-initialize your provider and contract instances because the network context has changed. Failing to handle these events leads to stale signer references and confusing behavior where actions are attempted with the wrong account or on the wrong chain. Always show clear UI feedback when these events happen so the user understands why controls may be disabled or state refreshed. A simple pattern is to re-run your initialization routine on these events so your front-end remains consistent with the wallet's current state. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Event Listeners
Listener patterns
window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (accounts) => {
  if (accounts.length === 0) {
    // user disconnected
  } else {
    // update signer and contract instances
  }
});

window.ethereum.on('chainChanged', (chainId) => {
  // recommended: reload or re-init provider/signer
  window.location.reload();
});
Reloading is a simple approach, but you can also programmatically re-initialize provider, signer and contracts for a smoother UX.
UI guidance
Notify the user immediately when accounts or chains change and show what decisions your app made in response.
Warning

Not handling account or chain changes yields stale signer usage and can cause transactions to be signed by the wrong account.

screens.title: Read vs Write: UX and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between read and write operations helps you design better UX and avoid unnecessary prompts. Reads, using view functions, are fast, free, and should be used to display state. Writes create transactions and require the user's explicit approval inside their wallet. From a UX perspective, minimize the number of wallet prompts and clearly separate actions that only read from those that will trigger a signature. For performance, batch reads or cache values for short periods when appropriate; for writes, always show a pending state and await confirmation. Also consider when to attach a provider versus a signer: attaching a provider avoids asking the wallet for permission until a write is needed. A common misconception is that calling functions with a signer is always harmful; it's not — but use signer only when necessary. Present clear messages like 'Confirm in MetaMask' and 'Transaction pending' so users are not surprised by pop-ups or delays. This comparison ensures predictable behavior and a trustworthy user interface. Read vs Write: UX and Performance means use provider for fast reads and signer only for required write operations; clearly surface transaction lifecycle to users.. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Defensive Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes disrupt front-end dApp flows. First, attempting to call window. ethereum. request without checking whether window. ethereum exists leads to runtime errors when a wallet is not installed. Always guard these calls and show an installation prompt if needed. Second, forgetting to await asynchronous operations, most notably tx. wait after a write, causes UI inconsistencies because your app may read state before a transaction is mined. Third, exposing private keys or signing directly in front-end code is insecure — all signing must happen inside the user's wallet. Defensive patterns include showing clear status messages for connection, pending transactions, and errors; disabling action buttons until a signer is available; and reinitializing signer and contracts on accountsChanged. Additionally, handle user rejections explicitly with friendly messaging rather than logging only to the console. These protective measures improve reliability and user trust, and they reduce support requests for confusing or broken dApp behavior. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how a web page becomes a decentralized application by using a browser wallet and a small JavaScript bridge library. Client-side libraries such as Web3. js and Ethers. js let your site ask the user to connect a wallet, create a provider to observe the chain, and obtain a signer to authorize state changes. You will see how the injected window. ethereum object is the entry point for MetaMask and similar wallets, how to request account access, and why the ABI and contract address are required to make calls from the browser. This matters because most users will interact with a dApp through a familiar web UI; wiring the front-end correctly gives reliable prompts, prevents common errors, and ensures signing happens safely inside the user's wallet. We will also cover read-only calls that are free and immediate, and write operations which produce a transaction that must be confirmed. By the end you will be able to build a small H T M L page that connects to MetaMask, shows a contract value, and sends a transaction while handling user confirmation and errors. Think about the first time you clicked a connect button — this lesson explains what happens under the hood and why awaiting confirmations is essential.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when building a browser-based dApp. First, you will be able to explain the role of client-side libraries like Web3. js and Ethers. js in bridging the browser and the blockchain, and you will know why they are needed. Second, you will learn the exact steps to detect and connect a user's wallet, using the injected window. ethereum object and a request for accounts. Third, you will obtain a Provider and a Signer from the connected wallet and understand their different capabilities: reads versus signed writes. Finally, you will call both view and state-changing functions on a deployed contract from a simple H T M L page while handling errors, user rejections, and pending transactions. Each objective is paired with a short explanation and a practical milestone so you can verify competency as you build. These skills matter because a clear, defensive front-end avoids broken user flows and keeps private keys inside the wallet rather than in your app.

In addition to A P I mechanics, you will practice UX and robust error handling that prevent common browser interaction failures. You will learn to detect when window. ethereum is missing and show a clear message to the user, to handle user rejection of account or transaction requests gracefully, and to respond to account and chain changes via event listeners. You will also understand the importance of waiting for transaction confirmation with tx. wait so the UI remains consistent with blockchain state. Finally, you'll build a minimal hands-on page with the ethers. js CDN, a connect button, and operations for a Counter contract. These learning goals emphasize that front-end dApp code must anticipate real user behavior: wallets not installed, users who cancel prompts, and network mismatches. Each objective includes a small verification step so you can confirm competency, for example by observing MetaMask pop-ups and a status field that updates while awaiting tx. wait. This makes your dApp both resilient and trustworthy to users.

Client-side libraries provide the glue your dApp needs to talk to the blockchain without exposing private keys. Ethers. js and Web3. js provide utilities to encode function calls, decode results, format values, and to route requests through a provider that speaks to the network. In the browser context they rely on a provider implementation surfaced by the user's wallet, commonly available as window. ethereum. A provider is effectively a read-only gateway that can query chain data and fetch on-chain state without requesting a signature. A signer is a thin wrapper around an account that can propose transactions and sign them inside the wallet. This separation matters: reads are cheap and immediate, writes require user confirmation and produce transactions that must be mined. A common misconception is that ethers. js holds keys for you on the client; it does not. In the browser, signing always occurs inside the wallet extension or mobile app. To ground this, imagine an online bank: the provider is like a public ledger viewer, the signer is like the customer approving a wire transfer in their secure banking app. The core insight is to treat the wallet as the secure signer and the library as a safe translator between your UI and that signer.

The first live step in most dApps is establishing a connection to the user's wallet. Start by checking whether window. ethereum exists. If it does not, the user likely has no Web3 wallet installed and you should surface a clear message. If it exists, call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts to prompt the user to connect. The promise resolves with an array of addresses when the user approves, or throws when the user rejects. This pattern keeps your app defensive and prevents runtime errors like 'cannot read request of undefined.' After successful connection, enable UI controls and instantiate a provider and signer. Remember to handle both success and failure: on rejection show a helpful message and offer a retry, and when accepted update the UI to show the connected address. Also register listeners for accountsChanged and chainChanged so your app adapts when the user switches accounts or networks. This makes the dApp robust across real user actions and avoids stale signer references. A misconception to avoid is assuming connection is permanent — the user can disconnect or switch accounts at any time.

Once a user approves connection, instantiate a provider that routes RPC calls through the wallet, and obtain a signer to authorize transactions. In ethers. js the pattern is creating a Web3Provider from window. ethereum and then calling getSigner on it. The provider lets you call view functions and read chain data; the signer represents the currently selected account and can sign and send transactions. It is common to use the signer when creating a contract instance intended for writes, and to use the provider for read-only interactions. A frequent subtlety is that after accounts change, you should re-acquire the signer from the provider to reflect the new selected account. Another common misunderstanding is confusing the provider returned by a JSON-RPC node and the Web3Provider wrapped around window. ethereum. The latter goes through the user's wallet and therefore triggers the wallet UI for signing. In practice you will see code like const provider = new ethers. providers. Web3Provider(window. ethereum); const signer = provider. getSigner(); — this small pattern is foundational for secure front-end interactions. Provider and Signer in ethers.js means web3provider wraps window.ethereum for reads; getsigner provides the user's account for signing transactions inside the wallet.. In practical terms, instantiate web3provider and getsigner from window.ethereum. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading state from a contract is straightforward and free because view functions do not create transactions. With an ethers. Contract instance attached to a provider you can call the view function and update the UI with the returned value. For example, to show a simple Counter contract's current count, call the count function and convert the returned BigNumber to a string for display. Handle errors such as network problems by wrapping calls in try/catch. Reads are typically fast and should be used to refresh UI state after transactions confirm, or periodically if your dApp requires near-real-time updates. A common pitfall is mistakenly creating the contract with a signer when you only need to read — this is not wrong, but it may trigger unwanted prompts if signer initialization requires user interaction. Keep read logic isolated and graceful: show a loading state while the read is in progress, show an error state if it fails, and never assume the read will always return immediately. This pattern gives users clear feedback and prevents confusing blank displays. Calling a view function (getCount) means attach the contract to a provider for free view calls; handle errors and show loading states for good ux.. In practical terms, read contract state without creating transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Write operations change blockchain state and therefore create transactions that must be signed and mined. When you call an increment function that is nonpayable, ethers. js returns a TransactionResponse immediately after the user confirms in their wallet. Understanding the difference between read and write operations helps you design better UX and avoid unnecessary prompts. Reads, using view functions, are fast, free, and should be used to display state. Writes create transactions and require the user's explicit approval inside their wallet. From a UX perspective, minimize the number of wallet prompts and clearly separate actions that only read from those that will trigger a signature. For performance, batch reads or cache values for short periods when appropriate; for writes, always show a pending state and await confirmation. Also consider when to attach a provider versus a signer: attaching a provider avoids asking the wallet for permission until a write is needed. Several recurring mistakes disrupt front-end dApp flows. First, attempting to call window. ethereum. request without checking whether window. ethereum exists leads to runtime errors when a wallet is not installed. Always guard these calls and show an installation prompt if needed. Second, forgetting to await asynchronous operations, most notably tx. wait after a write, causes UI inconsistencies because your app may read state before a transaction is mined. Third, exposing private keys or signing directly in front-end code is insecure — all signing must happen inside the user's wallet. Defensive patterns include showing clear status messages for connection, pending transactions, and errors; disabling action buttons until a signer is available; and reinitializing signer and contracts on accountsChanged.
